requirements.feature: Fabric calls retry only where retrying is provably safe, with server-side correlationId deduplication
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-33. FabricClient.call opened one connection, sent one request, and either returned or threw -- no retry anywhere -- while correlationId rode the wire frame purely to satisfy the sealed-interface shape and was never used for deduplication. A caller whose target died mid-call got an exception with no guidance on whether retrying was safe. Now a failure raised before the connection is established is wrapped as FabricConnectException and fails over to a different endpoint through the existing tier/version/breaker selection path whatever the method does (nothing ran, so nothing can duplicate); a failure after the request was written is retried only when the target method carries the new @Idempotent annotation, matched by annotation-type name so a module layer's own copy still counts. Attempts of one logical call share a correlationId, and FabricServer routes every inbound request through a bounded (4096), time-windowed (60s) InvocationDeduplicator that replays an already-answered id's response (InvokeError included) rather than re-executing, makes a duplicate arriving mid-flight wait on the original rather than race it, and deliberately does not remember an id whose dispatch threw. Bounded at MAX_CALL_ATTEMPTS=3; invokeByName has no resolved Method and is never retried past the write.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: InvocationDeduplicatorTest, FabricServerDeduplicationTest, FabricServiceRegistryRetryTest (+ RetryableGreeter fixture), FabricClientTest connect-time vs mid-call classification. FabricServiceRegistryTest's spillover test was changed from a refused port to an accept-then-hang-up endpoint so it still exercises a mid-call failure rather than being satisfied by the new connect-time failover.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature kills or partitions one of two provider replicas mid-call. Covering this needs a scenario that drops one greeter-provider replica during an in-flight call and asserts an idempotent call still succeeds through failover while a non-idempotent one surfaces the failure.

requirements.feature: Per-endpoint circuit breaker state is visible as logs and shipped Micrometer meters
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-78. CircuitBreaker.state() was called from nowhere outside the breaker's own transition logic -- no metric, API field or console indicator anywhere -- and the only externally visible trace of a trip was a single log line in the cluster-wide panic-mode branch, so an individual endpoint's breaker opening produced no log, metric or queryable state at all. CircuitBreaker gained a TransitionListener (notified outside its own lock, so a slow listener cannot stall a call path), FabricServiceRegistry logs every transition (WARN on open, INFO on half-open/close, naming the callee interface and nodeId/workerId), and WorkerMetrics registers gimle.fabric.circuitbreaker.state (gauge: 0 CLOSED, 1 HALF_OPEN, 2 OPEN) and gimle.fabric.circuitbreaker.transitions (counter tagged by state entered). Both ride the existing MeterSnapshotCodec -> agent -> Muninn path and are queryable through /metrics-history/*, so no new ControlMessage or heartbeat field was needed. Initial CLOSED state is published on breaker creation and meters are evicted when a breaker leaves the bounded per-endpoint map.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: CircuitBreakerTest (four listener tests: full open/half-open/close cycle, no-op calls report nothing, cooldown expiry seen only by a candidacy check still reported, failed half-open trial reports the re-open); FabricServiceRegistryRetryTest asserts the gauge level, the transition counter and the logged line via a Logback ListAppender.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature reads fabric breaker meters or log lines. Covering this needs a two-replica provider topology where one replica is killed and the scenario asserts that endpoint's gimle.fabric.circuitbreaker.state reaches 2 through the control plane's /metrics-history/* proxy.

requirements.feature: Cluster DNS answers NODATA, not NXDOMAIN, for a declared Service with no live endpoints
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-11. ControlPlaneServicePoller filtered a Service out of the cache entirely whenever its endpoint list was empty (.filter(endpoints -> !endpoints.endpoints().isEmpty())), so a Service mid-rollout or scaled to zero -- which ServiceReconciler's own javadoc calls a normal, valid outcome -- returned NXDOMAIN, contradicting SkaldServer's own javadoc preferring NOERROR/zero-answers for exactly this case. ServiceDirectory.resolveAll now returns Optional<List<HostPort>> so the two states are expressible at all: absent means no such name, present-but-empty means known Service with zero endpoints. The poller keeps empty Services; only a per-service 404 (the Service vanished between the catalog listing and the fetch) still drops a name. SkaldServer answers NXDOMAIN for an unknown name, NOERROR with zero answers for a known-and-empty one for both A and SRV queries, and SERVFAIL when the cached data is severely stale -- the zero-endpoint case included, since 'no endpoints' is itself a claim about current cluster state. A dashed per-endpoint name under an empty Service stays NXDOMAIN, which is correct: that specific name genuinely does not exist.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: SkaldServerTest (5 new: known-empty answers NOERROR for A and for SRV, unknown stays NXDOMAIN alongside a known-empty one, dashed endpoint name under an empty Service stays NXDOMAIN, severely stale empty is SERVFAIL); ControlPlaneServicePollerTest (a_service_with_no_endpoints_stays_in_the_cache_as_a_known_empty_name replaces the old test that asserted the defect); CachingServiceDirectoryTest (absent vs present-but-empty, and a refresh that empties a name keeps it known).
requirements.gapNote: No .feature boots a Skald replica at all, so nothing exercises a real DNS query. Covering this needs a topology with skald enabled plus a scenario that scales a Service's backing deployment to zero and asserts the RCODE flips between NOERROR and NXDOMAIN accordingly.

requirements.feature: Gateway TLS selects a per-virtual-host certificate from the client's SNI extension
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-52. TLS termination built one HttpsServer from a single SslContexts.forMutualTls(...) call at startup with no per-connection certificate selection, even though GatewayRouteConfig implements virtual hosting ([HOST <hostname>] route lines) and dispatch genuinely routes by the inbound Host header -- so with TLS on and more than one hostname routed, every host except the one the configured certificate's SAN covered failed validation for any client that checks hostnames. A new optional gateway.tlsCertificates config binds <hostname> <certFile> <keyFile> per line (same line/comment shape as gateway.routes), and a custom X509ExtendedKeyManager reads ExtendedSSLSession#getRequestedServerNames in chooseServerAlias/chooseEngineServerAlias to present the right certificate per connection. No SNIMatcher is installed, deliberately: a matcher refuses an unrecognized hostname, which would take host-unconstrained fallback routes down with it -- a client sending no SNI, and one naming an unbound hostname, both fall back to the cluster-wide certificate. The JSSE plumbing lives in gimle-core's existing com.gimle.core.tls as an overload whose empty-list case delegates to the existing single-certificate method, so the degenerate case is literally the previous code path.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: GatewayTlsConfigTest and GatewayHooksTlsTest (11 new): per-host certificate presented for each SNI name, no-SNI falls back to the cluster-wide certificate, an unbound hostname falls back rather than failing the handshake, wildcards/duplicate hostnames/wrong field counts/missing files rejected at parse time.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature boots a TLS-terminating gateway with two routed hostnames. Covering this needs a topology with a gateway in mTLS mode carrying two host-constrained routes plus per-host certificates, asserting each hostname validates.

requirements.feature: Autoscale policies carry scale-up and scale-down stabilization windows backed by durable last-scale state
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-10. Scale-up/down and multiple trigger metrics with combination modes were genuinely implemented, but no cooldown/stabilization field existed anywhere in the policy and AutoscaleReconciler adjusted by exactly +/-1 replica every tick off that tick's signal alone, with no 'time since last scale event' check in the class -- so a metric oscillating around its threshold could scale up, then down, then up indefinitely. AutoscalePolicy gained scaleUpCooldown and scaleDownCooldown Durations, defaulting asymmetrically the way operators expect (DEFAULT_SCALE_UP_COOLDOWN 0, so a load spike is answered on the next tick; DEFAULT_SCALE_DOWN_COOLDOWN 5 minutes, matching HPA's own scale-down stabilization default); explicit 0 disables a window and a negative value is rejected. Critically the 'time since last scale' is durable observed state, not a reconciler field: a new deploymentLastScale map in StateStore is written by a new StateMutation.PutDeploymentLastScale riding the same batch as the PutEffectiveReplicas it accounts for, replicated through RaftCodec (mutation and snapshot), readable over StoreRpc.GetDeploymentLastScale, and cleared on removeDeployment so a recreated name does not inherit an old window -- so the window survives a control-plane restart or failover and the reconciler stays level-triggered. Clamping an out-of-range stored replica count back into [minReplicas, maxReplicas] is computed separately from the signal-driven step and is deliberately never suppressed, since that is a bounds correction rather than a scaling decision.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: AutoscaleReconcilerTest (8 new, including the explicit oscillation test proving a scale-up cannot be reversed inside its window, a fresh-reconciler test proving the window is read from durable store state rather than instance state, convergence from a future-dated stamp left by a clock-skewed replica, and out-of-range clamping still applied while the signal step is suppressed); AutoscalePolicyTest, DeploymentManifestParserTest, StateStoreTest, RaftCodecTest, StoreCodecTest, ApiServerTest, ManifestExportTest.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature drives a metric across its target and back to observe the window suppressing the reversal. Covering this needs a scenario deploying with a short scaleDownCooldownSeconds, driving load up until the effective replica count rises, dropping it, and asserting through the real API that the count holds until the window elapses.

requirements.feature: CronJob schedules can be suspended without deleting and recreating them
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-54. CronJobSpec had no suspend/paused field and CronJobReconciler fired every non-terminal CronJob every tick with no pause check anywhere, so the only way to stop a schedule was delete-then-recreate, which cannot preserve prior firing history across the round trip. CronJobSpec gained a suspend boolean (manifest suspend:, default false), parsed, persisted through DomainCodec, surfaced on the API read side and in the CLI. A suspended CronJob records each due instant as it passes but plans no firing, so it keeps its history, stays listed, and unsuspending resumes at the next due instant rather than back-firing every missed schedule -- and it advances at its own schedule's cadence, not the reconcile loop's. History pruning still runs. triggerNow still fires a suspended CronJob, documented as deliberate since kubectl create job --from=cronjob/x behaves the same way.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: CronJobReconcilerTest (5 new: a suspended CronJob never fires from any starting tick; unsuspending resumes at the next due instant without back-firing the backlog; history is preserved across suspend/unsuspend; convergence from an arbitrary mid-schedule state; triggerNow still fires); CronJobManifestParserTest, ManifestExportTest.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature exercises CronJob suspension. Covering this needs a scenario that suspends a CronJob with a fast schedule, asserts no new Jobs appear across several intervals, then unsuspends and asserts exactly one fires.

requirements.feature: Health probe interval, timeout and liveness failure threshold are declarable per module
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-36. Probe interval (1s), timeout (2s) and liveness failure threshold (3) were literal constants applied identically to every module a worker hosts, and the manifest's health: block carried only initialDelaySeconds -- so a module whose readiness check needs more than two seconds (a cold cache fill, a slow downstream dependency) failed every readiness tick indistinguishably from a genuinely broken probe. The health: block gained intervalSeconds, timeoutSeconds and failureThreshold; HealthProbes carries them as Optional<Duration>/OptionalInt with a compact constructor enforcing positive interval and timeout, non-negative initial delay and threshold >= 1; the parser rejects zero, negative and non-numeric values with GimleManifestException. WorkerRuntime.onActive resolves each module's effective timing from its own descriptor with the worker default as fallback and records the effective liveness threshold per module at ACTIVE rather than re-reading it on failure, so a concurrent uninstall cannot strand the lookup. The three worker-wide constants are now explicitly named defaults.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: HealthProbesTest (9 new, every validation failure); ModuleDescriptorParserTest (8 added, including zero/negative/non-numeric for each field); WorkerRuntimeProbeTimingTest (5 new, real dynamically-loaded fixture modules through a real ModuleController/WorkerRuntime: a declared timeoutSeconds keeps a 400ms readiness check ready against a 100ms worker default while the same check without it is cut off; declared vs default failureThreshold; a declared long intervalSeconds suppresses fast-cadence probing).
requirements.gapNote: No .feature deploys a module declaring its own health timing. Covering this needs a fixture whose readiness probe is deliberately slower than the worker default, asserting it reaches ACTIVE only when its manifest declares a larger timeoutSeconds.

requirements.feature: Instance event history is cleared when a workload is removed, so a reused name starts clean
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-37. removeDeployment, removeDaemonSetSpec and removeStatefulSetSpec each explicitly cleared that workload's ControllerRevision history -- with removeDeployment's own javadoc spelling out exactly why a name reuse would otherwise bleed old history into a new, unrelated resource -- but instanceEvents, keyed by the identical (name, index) composite, had no equivalent cleanup anywhere, leaving the exact bug that cleanup was written to prevent live on its sibling structure. All three removal paths now call a private clearInstanceEventsFor(tenantId, name) beside the existing controllerRevisions.remove(...). The helper drops every instanceEvents key under the scoped key plus '#' whose remainder is all digits, so a similarly-named workload (orders vs orders#eu) is untouched. Because the cleanup lives inside the removal method the corresponding StateMutation applies, it rides the replicated Raft path rather than mutating a map behind the log, and the cleared timelines are consequently absent from snapshot() too.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: StateStoreTest (7 new: every index cleared; delete-then-recreate starts empty for all three workload kinds; another tenant's same-named timeline survives; a similarly-named workload survives; a cleared timeline does not return through a snapshot/restore round trip); MutationBatchTest (replaying PutDeployment, AppendInstanceEvent, RemoveDeployment, PutDeployment in log order on a fresh replica leaves the recreated name empty).
requirements.gapNote: No .feature deletes and recreates a workload under the same name to inspect its event timeline. Covering this needs a scenario asserting gimle events returns nothing for a freshly recreated name that previously had events.

requirements.feature: RBAC permissions accept a wildcard sentinel in the resource, verb and tenant-scope positions
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-58. No wildcard sentinel was recognized anywhere in com.gimle.core.authz -- --permission "*:read" threw a loud 400 -- and the only breadth mechanism was a fixed set of built-in templates hardcoded in Java source, so a role like 'read every resource kind across every tenant except SECRET' had to be hand-enumerated and re-edited every time a ResourceKind was added. Permission's resource and verb became Optional<ResourceKind>/Optional<Verb>, empty meaning every value -- the same 'absent constraint is unconstrained' semantics tenantScope already had, so all three positions read alike -- with Permission.ALL ("*") as the single written spelling and covers/coversResource/coversVerb doing the widening. The sentinel is persisted as a sentinel and expanded at authorize time, never at write time, so a grant automatically covers a ResourceKind added later without the stored role being rewritten. The qualifier position deliberately rejects the wildcard, so a wildcard resource grant still never reaches a {kind}/status write. Auditing every authorize call site found one parallel matcher: Authorizer.hasAnyReadGrant compared permission.resource()/verb() directly and would have silently denied the collection-list gate to a wildcard holder; it now delegates to the shared matching, so all defense-in-depth re-checkers (gimle-controlplane, gimle-fafnir, gimle-muninn, gimle-andvari, and gimle-agent's admin fault API) behave identically.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: PermissionTest (10 new: wildcard in each position, wildcard combined with a named value, token round-trip, malformed/blank/unknown input, wildcard-qualifier rejection, wildcard never reaching a {kind}/status write); WildcardPermissionAuthzTest (new, 11: every ResourceKind covered by one stored grant, the stored role staying a single unexpanded permission, codec round-trip preserving the wildcard, a narrower grant alongside a wildcard grant, hasAnyReadGrant, an unbound principal unaffected); GimleCliTest (3 added).
requirements.gapNote: No .feature creates a Role with a wildcard permission and asserts a bound subject's access against a real cluster; existing RBAC scenarios use fully-named grants only.

requirements.feature: Overlapping Services are announced with a response warning rather than silently allowed
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-34. Nothing checked a new ServiceSpec against any other Service's deploymentNames -- not the constructor, not ServiceRegistry.put, not the API handler -- so two Services naming the same Deployment each got their own live, correct-looking endpoint list pointed at the same instances, with nothing distinguishing an intentional shared front door from a typo and no console or CLI warning either. Because a shared front door is a legitimate pattern, this warns rather than rejects: the create still succeeds, and the control plane attaches an X-Gimle-Warning header naming each overlapping Service and the deployment names actually shared, which gimle set service and gimle apply -f print as a warning: line on stderr. No force or confirm flag was added.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: ServiceAdvisoriesTest (overlap reported; one warning per overlapping Service, name-ordered; a self re-submit does not overlap itself; the same deployment name under a different tenant is not an overlap; disjoint names earn nothing); ApiServerServicesTest (4 tests); GimleCliTest asserts the warning reaches stderr without failing the command.
requirements.gapNote: service-fabric.feature declares one Service and asserts it resolves a live endpoint; no scenario declares a second Service over the same deployment, and ServiceSteps discards the POST /services response headers entirely.

requirements.feature: A Service's targetPort is authoritative when declared and genuinely absent when not
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-53. targetPort was validated only for numeric range at admission and never against what any backing instance reported, and at resolution time ServiceEndpointResolver.resolve never read spec.targetPort() for the deployment-selector case at all -- solePort instead required the instance to report exactly one declared port and used it verbatim. So an operator could create a Service naming a targetPort no instance reports with no admission error, and the field had zero effect for any deployment reporting more than one port. targetPort is now OptionalInt and authoritative when declared: each backing instance contributes an endpoint on exactly that port, and an instance not reporting it is excluded with a logged reason (deduplicated per Service so a seconds-long tick does not spam) rather than quietly contributing a different port. Omitted, it is genuinely absent rather than defaulted to port: an instance reporting exactly one port contributes it, one reporting zero or several contributes nothing. Because instance ports are reported at runtime through ModuleContext.reportPort, a targetPort no instance currently reports cannot be a hard admission error -- it is level-triggered state -- so it is admitted with an X-Gimle-Warning instead. DomainCodec encodes 0 as undeclared, leaving the wire shape unchanged at one int.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: ServiceReconcilerTest (declared targetPort selects out of a multi-port instance; an instance not reporting it is excluded; no targetPort with exactly one reported port resolves; no targetPort with several stays ambiguous; a targetPort appearing and disappearing converges both ways; repeated ticks over an unchanged store keep producing the same endpoints); ApiServerServicesTest (5); ServiceAdvisoriesTest; ServiceSpecTest; GimleCliTest; console services repository tests.
requirements.gapNote: service-fabric.feature's one scenario declares targetPort 9500 against a module reporting exactly 9500, so it passes identically under both the old and new semantics and proves nothing about authority. Covering this needs a multi-port instance from which a declared targetPort selects one, and a declared targetPort the instance does not report.

requirements.feature: NetworkPolicy edits are version-guarded and can add or remove one allow-list entry at a time
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-12. NetworkPolicyRegistry exposed only whole-object put/get/list/remove -- no PATCH, no expectedVersion guard, unlike the sibling ConfigMap API's lease-guarded read-check-propose path -- and gimle set networkpolicy replaced the whole rule set too, so adding or removing one caller tenant meant GET-reconstruct-POST of the entire spec client-side: a lost-update race under any concurrent edit, and a client that omitted a field while reconstructing silently un-scoped the policy. The registry now follows the existing ConfigMap lease-guarded read-check-propose pattern rather than a new idiom, every write carries an expectedVersion guard that refuses a stale edit with 409, and the CLI gained --add-/--remove-allowed-caller-tenant and --add-/--remove-allowed-callee-tenant which read, amend and write under that guard.

holmgangScenarios.scenario: A concurrent edit against a stale version is refused instead of silently winning
holmgangScenarios.whyThisCounts: Against a real multi-replica cluster: creates a policy through control-plane replica 0, amends it to add a second caller tenant, asserts a second edit made against the version the first started from is rejected with 409, then reads the policy back through replica 1 and asserts both caller tenants are present -- proving the expectedVersion guard actually refuses a lost update and that the amended state is durable across replicas, not just locally applied.

requirements.otherTestCoverage: NetworkPolicyRegistryTest (the actual lost-update race, not just the happy path), ApiServerNetworkPoliciesTest, GimleCliTest.

requirements.feature: A NetworkPolicy may only name tenants that exist
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-35. NetworkPolicySpec's compact constructor validated the blankness and shape of allowedCallerTenantIds/allowedCalleeTenantIds but never checked any listed tenant ID against a real tenant registry, and neither did the registry's put nor the API handler -- so a typo'd or since-deleted tenant ID was silently accepted as a permanently-unreachable or dangling rule. Existence is now checked at admission in the API handler, which is the only layer that can reach a tenant registry; the record's compact constructor stays a pure shape check, since a record cannot and should not reach a registry.

holmgangScenarios.scenario: A policy naming a tenant that does not exist is refused
holmgangScenarios.whyThisCounts: Against a real running cluster, creating a network policy whose allow list names a tenant that was never created is rejected with 400 -- proving the admission-time existence check runs on the real API path rather than only in a unit-level registry test.

requirements.otherTestCoverage: ApiServerNetworkPoliciesTest; GimleCliTest's networkpolicy round-trip tests now declare the tenants their policies name.

requirements.feature: A tenant can be closed to cross-tenant fabric calls before its first NetworkPolicy exists
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-77. Every enforcement check consulted only the current, possibly-empty networkPolicies list, so an empty list -- every brand-new tenant's starting state -- meant the check loop never ran and nothing was ever denied. That matches the documented deny-by-default-once-a-policy-exists design exactly; the gap was that no per-tenant posture flag or deny-all shorthand existed to flip a new tenant closed beforehand. Tenant gained an isolationPosture of OPEN (the default, so existing behavior is unchanged unless an operator opts in) or DENY_BY_DEFAULT, under which an empty policy set denies rather than permits. It is set through gimle set tenant --isolation-posture, relayed to every worker on the same NetworkPolicyRelay -> ControlMessage.NetworkPoliciesUpdated path the policies themselves ride (via a new denyByDefaultTenantIds field and a new /networkpostures endpoint the agent polls), and re-checked independently by FabricServer. BifrostProxy consumes it too, keeping its documented fail-closed posture coherent for a deny-by-default tenant.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: ControlMessageCodecTest, NetworkPolicyRelayTest, HttpNetworkPolicySourceTest (including a test asserting only tenants declaring deny-by-default are reported closed), BifrostProxyTest, FabricServerTest.
requirements.gapNote: network-policy.feature gained scenarios for the version guard and the unknown-tenant refusal but none for the posture itself. Covering this needs a scenario booting a DENY_BY_DEFAULT tenant with an empty policy set, asserting a cross-tenant fabric call is refused, plus the OPEN control case proving the same call succeeds -- which is the entire behavioral claim of this item.

requirements.feature: Every secret version records who wrote it, when, and its declared type
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-19. secret versions returned bare version integers only -- neither the Meta pointer record nor the underlying ConfigEntry carried a timestamp or author -- and while the audit trail captured principal and timestamp at write time it never captured the resulting version number, with GET /audit offering no key filter. Each version now records the writing principal, the wall-clock write time and its declared type on the key@meta pointer's append-only versions list, returned by the version listing and by a single-key read; the write's own audit event now carries the version it produced, via a new append-only OptionalInt version field on AuditEvent encoded at the end of DomainCodec's existing encoding with no format-version constant bumped.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: SecretStoreTest (author and timestamp on every version; soft delete and undelete leave write history intact; versionInfo for a missing version is empty); FafnirServerTest; AuditEventTest (a versioned write carries its version; an unversioned resource kind carries none; a null version coalesces to empty); SecretCommandTest; console repository and store tests.
requirements.gapNote: secrets-and-pki.feature exercises version numbers only. Covering this needs a step that writes a secret as a known principal over mTLS and asserts both the version listing's author/timestamp and the matching AuditEvent's version.

requirements.feature: A secret write may declare its value's shape, validated before anything is stored
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-60. validateKey checked only the key name; the plaintext value was encrypted and stored completely unexamined, and no secret type concept existed anywhere in the platform, so a value a manifest would later mount as a TLS key or certificate was accepted with no shape validation at write time. A write may now declare a type -- opaque (the default, and the only unvalidated one), pem-certificate, or pem-private-key -- validated structurally before anything is encrypted or stored, with the type persisted per version and reported on read. The private-key type accepts every openssl-emitted label (PKCS#8, PKCS#1, SEC1, encrypted), since rejecting a valid key purely for its label would make the type useless for real material. The CLI gained --type and --from-file, the latter because a multi-line PEM cannot otherwise be supplied.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: SecretTypeTest (new, 12: wire-name parsing, opaque accepts anything, missing/truncated/empty-body/non-base64 PEM rejection, every openssl private-key label accepted, mismatched begin/end labels rejected, a certificate refused where a private key was declared); SecretStoreTest (4); FafnirServerTest (malformed rejected with 400 and never stored; unknown type rejected); SecretCommandTest (3); console tests.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature writes a typed secret. Covering this needs a scenario writing a well-formed PEM certificate with --type through the real CLI and a truncated one expecting a nonzero exit and no stored version.

requirements.feature: A tenant's whole secret set can be exported and imported in one authorized, audited call
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-71. Every read verb was strictly one key or map at a time and list endpoints returned metadata or names only, never values; Fafnir's backend already had a bulk-value endpoint but it existed solely for gimle-agent's internal fetch and no CLI verb wrapped it. SecretStore.getMany now serves a whole batch from one store listing, exposed as GET /secrets/{tenantId}?names=a,b,c behind a dedicated authorizeSecretsBulkRead, and the CLI gained export and import. The security posture was treated as the deliverable rather than the test count: the bulk read runs Fafnir's own independent Authorizer.authorize check, is deliberately not routed through the node self-service short-circuit and refuses any gimle:nodes principal outright so the path never widens a node identity's reach, and both allow and deny are audited. A key that is unknown or soft-deleted is omitted rather than failing the whole batch. At-rest posture, deliberate and documented: the export file holds plaintext material, base64-encoded but not encrypted, because ciphertext under the source cluster's master key is useless at a destination with a different one -- which is the whole reason the command exists. Compensating constraints: the destination must be a file, never stdout; it is created rw------- where POSIX permissions exist; an existing path is refused rather than overwritten; and deleting the file after import is stated as the operator's responsibility in both the CLI output and the docs.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: SecretStoreTest (2); FafnirServerTest (2); FafnirSecretsAuthzTest (the bulk read runs its own authorizer check and forbids an ungranted caller; is allowed for a caller holding SECRET read; a node is forbidden the bulk read even with an active assignment while keeping its single-key read); SecretCommandTest (5, including owner-only file mode, refusal to overwrite, and a soft-deleted secret omitted).
requirements.gapNote: No .feature exercises a bulk secret read. Covering this needs a scenario exporting a tenant's secrets through the real CLI, importing them into a second tenant and asserting the round trip, plus an mTLS variant asserting a node identity is refused the ?names= route.

requirements.feature: Secret and config payloads are bounded on both the value and the raw request body
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-72. Neither a secret's plaintext nor a config value's byte length was checked anywhere in the write path, and the HTTP body itself was read unbounded via readAllBytes() with no Content-Length cap in both FafnirServer and ApiServer; the only nearby admission guardrails check CPU, memory and instance counts, never payload size. Limits are now enforced at both layers: ConfigEntry.MAX_VALUE_BYTES is 1 MiB (the storage row ceiling, matching Kubernetes' own Secret/ConfigMap limit), SecretStore.MAX_VALUE_BYTES and ApiServer.MAX_CONFIG_VALUE_BYTES are 512 KiB (half of it, so a value accepted at write time still fits once encrypted), and request bodies are capped at 4 MiB in both servers using the existing com.gimle.core.io.SizeLimitedInputStream on the streamed bytes rather than trusting Content-Length -- so an oversized body is refused before it is buffered whole.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: ApiServerPayloadLimitTest (new), SecretStoreTest and FafnirServerTest boundary cases on both the value-length and request-body paths.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature attempts an oversized secret or config write. Covering this needs a scenario writing a value past the ceiling through the real API and asserting the refusal.

requirements.feature: Logs can be filtered by level threshold and text at the reader, on every surface
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-38. LogFileReader, the shared primitive behind every log route, filtered only by timestamp cursor -- no level or text parameter existed anywhere in its signature -- so the CLI accepted only --category/--follow/--since and the console coloured a line by level after the fact but never filtered by it. A new LogFilter record in gimle-core carries both predicates and is taken by every log reader, so both surfaces get filtering from one mechanism rather than two implementations. Level is a threshold (TRACE < DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR); a line with no level, or one off that scale such as a raw SYSTEM capture, cannot be ranked and is excluded rather than silently admitted, and an unrecognized level is a 400 naming the accepted values. Text is plain case-insensitive substring, deliberately not regex, matched against message/logger/stackTrace/raw only and never nodeId/thread where a short query would match every line from one node. Filtering happens server-side at the reader so a high-volume log is not shipped in full; the filter is applied before limit, so a page is the last N matching lines; and streamFollow suppresses non-matching lines while still advancing its cursor past them so a quiet run is not re-scanned every tick. The parameters thread through AgentLogServer, the ApiServer /logs/* proxy and the Muninn fallback identically, so an operator gets the same result whether or not the owning node is still alive. A zero-match query is legible on every surface rather than silent.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: LogFilterTest (18), LogFileReaderFilteringTest (8), AgentLogServerTest (7 new), MuninnDayFileStoreTest, MuninnLogFilterParityTest (6 -- asserts the Muninn fallback returns exactly what the live-agent reader returns for the same lines and filter), ApiServerLogsFallbackTest (7 new), LogsCommandTest (7), and 43 console Vitest cases across lib, route, Mock and Http repository tests.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature reads logs through /logs/* at all; the one log-facing step greps agent-platform.log off disk and never exercises the API. Covering this needs a scenario tailing a deployed module's log through the real API with a level threshold and asserting only matching lines return.

requirements.feature: A deleted config or secret key is retracted from a running instance, and modules can subscribe to changes
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-39. Config and secret hot-reload was real and push-based, but ConfigRelay relayed only creates and updates -- its own comment confirmed a key deleted upstream was deliberately never retracted from a running instance -- so deleting a key to revoke it had no effect until restart, leaving the stale value live and readable indefinitely. Separately ModuleContext exposed only pull-based config(key)/configKeys(), documented as a snapshot rather than a live view, with no listener a module could register, so a module wanting to react to a rotated credential had only its own polling. Retraction is now real and level-triggered: the relay delivers the authoritative current key set (ControlMessage.ConfigKeysRetained) so an instance converges from any starting state rather than depending on a delete event it might have missed, and a hosted module may register a listener called on every delivery, rotation and retraction of a key it can see. The javadoc and comments that documented non-retraction and the snapshot-only view as deliberate choices were rewritten, since leaving them would make the code lie about itself.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: ModuleConfigRetractionTest (new, including convergence from an arbitrary starting state rather than only a clean delete event), ConfigRelayTest, ControlMessageCodecTest.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature deletes a config or secret key while an instance is running. Covering this needs a scenario that deploys a module reading a key, deletes it, and asserts through the module's own log that the value is gone without a restart.

requirements.feature: Trace sampling is configurable and parent-based
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-59. Every SdkTracerProvider was built with no setSampler call, so the OTel SDK default of Sampler.alwaysOn() applied; no sampler configuration existed anywhere in the codebase and, unlike other deliberate defaults here, 100% sampling was never called out as an intentional choice in the observability docs. The recorded fraction is now configurable per process via -Dgimle.tracing.samplingRatio (0.0-1.0, default 1.0, so existing behavior is unchanged unless an operator opts in), honoured identically by every tracer-provider install path. The decision is parent-based, which is what keeps a trace whole across process hops -- sampling each hop independently would shred a cross-worker trace into disconnected fragments, which is precisely the trace this platform most needs to be readable.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: GimleTracingSamplingTest (new): default ratio records everything, a configured ratio is honoured on every install path, an out-of-range or non-numeric ratio is rejected, and a child span follows its parent's sampling decision rather than re-deciding.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature asserts trace volume or sampling. Covering this needs a scenario setting a ratio on a real cluster and asserting the shipped span count through /traces-history/*.

requirements.feature: Logs, metrics and traces each retain for their own configurable window
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-82. The only retention config was one gimle.muninn.retentionDays property feeding one RetentionSweeper that walked the entire data root and deleted any day file older than the cutoff, with no branch on whether the file lived under the logs, metrics or traces subtree -- so signals with very different reasonable retention needs shared a single global knob. Each signal now has its own window (gimle.muninn.logs.retentionDays, gimle.muninn.metrics.retentionDays, gimle.muninn.traces.retentionDays), each defaulting to the existing global gimle.muninn.retentionDays when unset, with anything outside the three known signal subtrees still swept on the global window.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: RetentionSweeperTest: each subtree swept on its own cutoff, a signal without an override follows the global window, an unknown subtree follows the global window, and sweeping twice or sweeping a missing data root stays a safe no-op.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature exercises retention sweeping at all. Covering this needs a scenario with short per-signal windows asserting differential deletion against a real Muninn replica.

requirements.feature: A trace can be followed across processes from the console's Traces screen
requirements.statusNote: Modified: the console followed a trace by paging backwards through each process separately; it now uses the control plane's one cross-process trace search, and reports a truncated or failed search rather than an incomplete trace.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: gimle-console/src/routes/-trace-follow.test.ts: spans grouped by process and nested by parent, an unreachable process reported rather than silently omitted, a trace present in only one process rendered without implying more. `-trace-follow.test.ts` was rewritten against the single search, and `tracesHistory.test.ts` covers the repository call.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature drives the console. The Playwright suite in gimle-console/e2e is the natural home; it does not yet cover the Traces screen.

requirements.feature: The one-time bootstrap password never reaches a build log or any other persistent sink
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes BETA-15. The password was printed with a plain System.out.println, and the Maven goal shelling the bootstrap out used ProcessBuilder(...).inheritIO(), making the subprocess's stdout Maven's own stdout -- indistinguishable from an interactive human run and captured verbatim into any pipeline's persistent build log. Auditing every path the generated password reaches found five sinks, not the one originally reported: the direct println; GimleProcesses/TlsInitMojo's inheritIO into the Maven build log; BootstrapMojo's runTlsInit and printSummary into the same; PkiInit.runOneShot, which redirects the subprocess into a durable pki-init.log file (confirming the suspected log-file leak); and gimle-holmgang's GimleCluster.generateTlsMaterial, the same shape into pki.log. The mechanism is terminal-or-explicit-file, refuse otherwise: the password prints only when stdout is genuinely a terminal, which stays true for a human running the goal in a shell and is false for any redirected or captured run; otherwise the caller must name --password-file, which is written alone with owner-only permissions and only its path printed; and with neither, the run is refused up front before any material is generated, naming the flag. That makes the automated case explicit rather than silently degrading into either a logged password or a lost one. RemoteDispatch was verified to copy named files only, so the password file never ships to fleet machines.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: PkiBootstrapMainTest (9): file-mode delivery, the password absent from the captured stream, the written password verifying against bootstrap-account.yaml's hash, owner-only file mode, refusal generating nothing at all, and interactive mode printing without writing a file. PkiInitTest (18) covers the hilmir path.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature provisions a cluster through the bootstrap goal and inspects its output for the password. Covering this needs a scenario running the bootstrap non-interactively and asserting the password appears only in the named file.

requirements.feature: The unauthenticated CSR bootstrap endpoint is rate limited
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes BETA-16. POST /bootstrap/csr had no rate limiting by explicit design -- PendingCsrStore's own javadoc said pruning by age bounded unbounded growth without needing real rate limiting for this pass -- while doing real asymmetric-crypto and parsing work per request with zero authentication. The existing com.gimle.core.throttle idiom was followed rather than a second one invented, but LoginThrottle is failure backoff and is useless where every expensive request succeeds, so a sibling RequestRateLimiter (token bucket, same in-memory per-replica posture, same Optional<Instant> shape so it plugs into the existing throttled-response path returning 429 with Retry-After) was added beside it, with no new dependency. Two buckets are charged before the request body is read -- the only placement that actually protects the work -- one per remote address and one cluster-wide, all four parameters tunable. They are sized deliberately high on a real constraint: a joining agent treats a rejected CSR as fatal and never retries, and an entire fleet can arrive from one address behind NAT. PendingCsrStore's javadoc, which documented the absence of rate limiting as deliberate, was rewritten to describe age-pruning as the complementary memory bound.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: RequestRateLimiterTest (8): burst, refusal with a retry instant, no lockout extension, refill, capacity cap, 200 distinct keys admitted while one is exhausted, exact admission count under 64 concurrent virtual threads, argument validation. BootstrapCsrRateLimitTest (4), including the explicit legitimate-fleet case: 50 simultaneous submissions from one address at shipped defaults, all accepted.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature floods the CSR endpoint. Covering this needs a scenario submitting past the burst against a real control plane and asserting the 429, alongside the existing agent CSR bootstrap scenarios proving a legitimate fleet still joins.

requirements.feature: Placement and quota failures name the resource dimension, the numbers and the shortfall
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes BETA-18. Placement and quota failures named the cause but not the remediation -- no resource dimension, no by-how-much -- unlike the node-taint conflict message, which deliberately names the specific conflicting node and tenant and was the quality bar to match. GimleSchedulingException's single catch-all noFeasiblePlacement was replaced by cause-specific factories, each raised at the stage that actually eliminated the last candidate: insufficientNodeCapacity names the short dimension and shortfall, the roomiest candidate and per-node free capacity (capped at five nodes with the remainder counted); noNodeSupportsTier lists what each node does support and says outright that adding capacity cannot help; noNodesRegistered is distinct from a shortfall; nodeCordoned and requiredLabelsUnsatisfied name the blocking nodes and the labels each node carries; and stickyNodeUnavailable, previously a list of six maybes, now names the one check the sticky node actually failed. The case where both dimensions fit somewhere but no single node fits both is reported as itself rather than as a fabricated shortfall, so a message never claims a cause the scheduler did not observe. On the quota side TenantUsage.describeOverage names every tripped dimension with its ceiling, the overage, and the already-assigned versus this-submission split. Supporting this, ResourceQuantity gained formatMemory/formatCpu -- the inverse of the existing parsers -- so computed byte and millicore values render in manifest units and round-trip back. Note the finding's accompanying claim that LimitRange violations share this problem was verified and is false: LimitRangeSpec.violation already names the side, the dimension, the actual value, the direction and the bound, so it was deliberately left unchanged.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: SchedulerDiagnosticsTest (new, 16 -- one per distinct elimination cause, asserting the exact wording and numbers, which is the deliverable here rather than incidental); TenantQuotaPluginTest (2 updated to the full new text, 4 added); ResourceSpecTest (new, 5, formatter/parser round trip).
requirements.gapNote: scheduling.feature exercises cordoning behaviourally but never reads the diagnostic text, and there is no quota-rejection feature at all. Covering this needs a scenario asserting the message content of a capacity rejection and of a quota rejection through the real API.

requirements.feature: A failing certificate rotation check is durably visible with a failure streak, metrics and remaining validity
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes BETA-19. A failed rotation check only logged a warning and silently kept the still-valid old certificate -- no alert-worthy signal, no visible next-check schedule -- which is harmless while the old certificate remains valid and exactly the failure mode that turns into a surprise expiry later. The check now produces a result instead of swallowing failures: CertificateRotationOutcome (DISABLED/NOT_DUE/ROTATED/FAILED) and CertificateRotationStatus (outcome, the current certificate's notAfter, consecutive-failure count, failure message, next-check time and remaining validity), with CertificateRotationMonitor owning the streak counter, escalating log lines (first failure WARN, third ERROR, then re-logged at most once a minute, each naming the error, the streak length, 'still valid until X' with the runway remaining, and the next attempt) and listener fan-out that can never break the rotation loop. Two previously silent no-ops became real failures along the way: a due certificate with no CSR endpoint configured, and a 200 response carrying no certificate. Metrics register gimle.certificate.rotation.consecutive.failures and gimle.certificate.remaining.seconds as gauges at construction -- so a healthy process reads an explicit 0 rather than an absent meter, since a metric that only exists once something is broken cannot be alerted on -- plus a checks counter tagged by outcome, riding the established MeterSnapshotCodec path to Muninn and queryable via /metrics-history/*. A durable audit event is appended only at the start and the escalation point of a streak, since checks run every two seconds and auditing every failure would flood the trail. Wired into all six rotating processes rather than only the reported call site. Deliberately not wired into the AlertRule primitive, which would require a new Metric enum value, an InstanceObservation field and heartbeat/codec changes.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature drives a failing rotation. Covering this needs a scenario pointing a process at an unreachable CSR endpoint with rotation due and asserting the failure gauge through /metrics-history/*.

requirements.feature: Tier-1 worker density is an operator-configurable, validated knob
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes BETA-17's configurability half. Tier-1 density was the hardcoded constant MAX_TIER1_DENSITY (4), whose own javadoc called it a simple constant to start, not a configurable knob yet. It became DEFAULT_MAX_TIER1_DENSITY (still 4) plus the gimle.agent.maxTier1Density property, following the same system-property convention the agent's other operator-facing settings already use, parsed and validated in main() before anything is supervised -- zero, negative or non-numeric throws at startup rather than silently reverting to the default -- and threaded through reconcileAssignments into findReusableTier1Worker. The javadoc calling it 'not a configurable knob yet' was rewritten to describe the knob and why 4 is conservative rather than measured. The accompanying documentation gap was closed with a new node-sizing reference page covering what runs on a node, where a worker's -Xmx and ActiveProcessorCount come from versus what capacity accounting uses, and the three consequences of raising density: a shared worker's ceiling is fixed at spawn time and never subdivided, density multiplies one worker's blast radius, and a leaking module hurts its neighbours. It states explicitly that it contains no measured benchmark numbers rather than inventing any.

requirements.feature: Gateway route-table and server fields are guarded under one monitor
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: found while integrating this change set, and pre-existing on master -- gimle-gateway failed spotbugs:check with two IS2_INCONSISTENT_SYNC findings, which meant mvn verify from the repo root was red on master and nothing downstream of gimle-gateway in the reactor had been verified at all. The findings were real rather than noise: appliedRoutesConfig and registeredPaths were written in onStart and in the synchronized reloadRoutesIfChanged, with the class comment asserting safety informally, but the route-reload scheduler is started by onStart and can tick before it returns -- so the happens-before rested on thread-start ordering the code never actually established. onStart now holds the same monitor across the bind, so the first tick waits for a fully-applied route table rather than reconciling contexts against a half-populated one; onStop and the port accessor take it too, since a reload tick in flight reads the very server onStop closes.

requirements.feature: A closed Bifrost service listener never serves one more connection
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: found while finishing this change set's test pass. ServiceListener.close() set closed, closed the ServerSocket and returned while its accept loop could still be blocked inside accept(); closing a ServerSocket does not retract a connection the kernel has already completed, so a listener dropped by BifrostProxy -- because the Service was removed, or the proxy was shutting down -- could accept and proxy one more caller after being dropped. Reproduced with a standalone java.net-only program independent of any Gimle code at roughly 8% of iterations, some connections even reading the payload the supposedly-closed accept loop wrote; zero occurrences in 500 iterations after the fix, and twelve consecutive clean suite runs. close() now joins the accept thread and re-checks closed immediately after accept() returns, so a raced connection is dropped rather than forwarded. This does not collide with the fail-closed policy path, which refuses connections on a live listener; the join concerns only a listener being torn down.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: BifrostProxyTest.a_service_disappearing_from_the_source_closes_its_listener, verified over twelve consecutive runs with no surefire flakes.
requirements.gapNote: No .feature exercises a Bifrost listener teardown race. Covering this needs a scenario removing a Service while a caller connects and asserting no further connection is served.

requirements.feature: Proxied query parameters are URL-encoded rather than relayed decoded

ApiServer.forwardedQuery relayed already-decoded query values verbatim when building the upstream URI, so the first parameter able to contain a space -- the new log text filter -- produced an invalid URI and a server error. It now URL-encodes keys and values when reconstructing the forwarded query. A latent defect rather than a new one: no pre-existing proxied parameter happened to contain a character requiring encoding.

requirements.feature: LimitRange management in the web console
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-15. LimitRange CRUD was fully covered by the CLI's LimitRangeCommand while the console had no LimitRange screen or repository at all -- the only trace anywhere in gimle-console/src was a read-only violation badge on the Deployments list, derived from deployment status rather than the resource itself. requirements.feature: Volumes screen: see and reclaim orphaned StatefulSet volumes
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-16. GET /volumes and DELETE /volumes/* were fully covered by the CLI's VolumesCommand while the console had no volumes repository or route -- the only mention of 'volume' anywhere was a warning sentence inside a StatefulSet delete dialog. requirements.feature: Seal-key lifecycle in the web console
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-17. The seal-key lifecycle (GET /seal/public-key, POST /seal/rotate-key, POST /seal/retire-key) was fully covered by the CLI's SealCommand with zero console presence. The screen shows the active key's id and algorithm and its base64 X.509 SubjectPublicKeyInfo with a copy action, displayed as-is rather than parsed or prettified. requirements.feature: Per-deployment metrics rollup on the Metrics screen
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-13's console half. The per-deployment rollup at GET /metrics was unreachable from either surface -- the console's Metrics screen derived its charts entirely from other stores and no metrics repository existed. requirements.feature: Live permission vocabulary endpoint driving the console's Roles picker
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-40. The console's Roles resource picker was a fixed Select sourced from an 18-value list while com.gimle.core.authz.ResourceKind holds 26 -- missing ALERT_RULE, BACKUP, CONFIGMAP, CUSTOM_RESOURCE, FAULT, KIND_DEFINITION, LIMIT_RANGE and SECRETMAP, so an operator delegating 'read this tenant's ConfigMaps but not its Secrets', or scoping a LimitRange or FAULT grant, could only do it from the CLI. The endpoint is gated consistently with its neighbour /authz/can-i -- under mTLS a caller must authenticate, but no grant is required and nothing is audited -- because the answer is a compile-time constant identical for every principal, revealing no cluster state and no hint of who may do what, and requiring a grant would break the picker for the very operator being asked to choose from it.

requirements.feature: An expired console session is explained once, in plain language
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-57. A 401 correctly cleared auth state and redirected to /login, but nothing explained why -- no session-expired string existed anywhere in the console and the login screen could not distinguish a fresh visit from a bounced one -- while the triggering action independently fired a raw toast carrying the literal ApiError text 'control plane responded 401: ...'. A 401 now throws a dedicated SessionExpiredError carrying a plain-language message, thrown centrally so any catch site that only reads error.message still shows a sentence rather than the raw status text; the shared error helpers toast nothing at all for a 401 while still toasting everything else. The auth store records that a real signed-in principal was bounced, and the login screen renders a session-expired notice, suppressed when the screen has its own sign-in error so the two never stack. A 403 still surfaces in place as a permission message, since that user is legitimately logged in and merely lacks one permission.

requirements.feature: Console screens keep themselves current
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-70. Auto-refresh existed only behind the Metrics/Traces go-live toggle; every workload and topology screen fetched once on mount and offered only a manual Refresh, so any reconciler-driven change was invisible until an operator acted. A shared poller now runs on a ten-second interval, on by default, behind a global switch persisted alongside the console's other display preferences. Rather than adding a second notion of live, the existing Metrics/Traces live polls and the Logs follow were rewritten onto the same poller and the global switch made master over them, so no screen carries two independent pollers. The poller skips rather than queues a tick whose predecessor is still in flight, stops on unmount, pauses while the tab is hidden and re-reads once on return, and holds its callbacks in refs so a re-render cannot reset the interval phase. Each store's poll is non-destructive: it never blanks the list, never raises the loading flag, requests at least as many rows as are already displayed so paged-in rows survive, keeps last-good data on failure, and stands aside while a manual load or a dirty form is in flight. Screens showing operator-authored configuration, and the destructive Seal Keys surface, are deliberately not polled.

The unreachable-nodes advisory in the volume listing was neither converted nor dropped: it is diagnostic rather than result data, and folding it into the body would force volume list to emit an object wrapper instead of the bare array every other list command emits, so it moved to stderr following the precedent already set for deprecation warnings -- stdout's own table or JSON output stays clean either way.

requirements.feature: A failed invocation exits with a code naming why it failed
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-79. A CliExitCode enum now defines 1 generic, 2 invalid input, 3 not found, 4 forbidden, 5 conflict and 6 unreachable or retryable, carried on CliException as a classification rather than a subtype hierarchy so the type stays final and five near-empty subclasses are avoided. describeError became errorFrom, returning the classified exception rather than a message string, and every IOException transport path throws the unreachable classification. 401 and 403 were not in the original switch at all and fell through to a bare unexpected-response message; both are now explicit and both map to forbidden, deliberately sharing a code because both mean the caller may not do this and no remedy depends on telling them apart. requirements.feature: gimle context: pointing the CLI at more than one cluster
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-42. The only ways to select a cluster were the --server flag or the GIMLE_SERVER environment variable, parsed fresh on every invocation, with no config file and no context subcommand anywhere. A context command now manages a config file holding named endpoints, and resolution follows a fixed precedence -- --server, then GIMLE_SERVER, then the current context -- with each rung read only when every earlier one is absent, which is also what keeps a broken config file from costing anything on an explicit invocation. The context verbs themselves run before any server is resolved, since they are what an operator uses before one exists. A missing file is the normal case and is never created until a first write; a malformed one degrades to a warning on stderr plus the ordinary no-server-configured error, while the context verbs report it as a hard error naming the file. The file stores endpoints only and never credentials, is written temp-file-then-atomic-move, and is created owner-only with an owner-only parent directory where POSIX permissions are supported.

requirements.feature: The audit trail pages with an eviction-safe cursor
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-41. The Audit screen used a flat user-editable limit with no cursor while GET /audit returned events with no paging metadata, so past the limit matching events were unreachable except by narrowing filters, with no signal anything had been cut off. The trail is a ring buffer that moves at both ends, which is precisely what defeats an offset cursor: appends at the newest end shift every offset and cause a page to skip rows, while evictions at the oldest end shift them back and cause rows to repeat. The cursor therefore names an event rather than a position, pairing the event id with a fingerprint of the filter values. The fingerprint is what makes the failure case unambiguous -- without it a missing anchor could mean either eviction or a caller changing filters between pages, which need opposite answers -- so a cursor presented with different filters is rejected outright and a missing anchor can then only mean eviction. Because eviction is strictly oldest-first, an evicted anchor implies everything older is gone too, so the response reports the walk as expired with an empty page rather than guessing. That signal stays distinct from the existing whole-trail truncation fields, and both surfaces render them separately. Cursor resolution and page slicing happen against one store snapshot, so no concurrent append or eviction can land between the lookup and the cut.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: AuditPageTest (8), ApiServerAuditPaginationTest (7) including a real eviction -- the ring is flooded until its cap has genuinely discarded the anchor, then the next page is fetched -- AuditCommandTest (5), plus console route and store tests (13).
requirements.gapNote: No .feature scenario reads GET /audit. Covering the eviction path additionally needs a topology knob for the store's fixed event cap. Unit/integration coverage listed in otherTestCoverage does not count toward RTM coverage per this file's own coverageRule.

requirements.feature: gimle get --watch observes a resource converging
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-69. --follow existed only for logs; every other read was a point-in-time snapshot, so watching a rollout, scale-up or cordon land meant a manual loop, with no equivalent of the obvious kubectl comparison. Watch is a client-side poll reusing the established follow idiom, since no streaming API exists outside logs. Each tick after the first prints a diff rather than the whole table -- re-printing eighty unchanged rows every interval is unreadable, and the operator cares about the two that moved -- under a header printed once, with an explicit event column. That column earns its place because a deletion is otherwise inexpressible: a poll-derived diff has nowhere else to say a row vanished, and re-printing the survivors cannot convey it. Row identity resolves through an ordered candidate field-set list falling back to whole-row content, so an unrecognised shape still diffs correctly, just as a delete plus an add rather than one modification. Under -o json the output is NDJSON matching the sibling logs --follow decision, wrapped in an envelope because the event kind is derived by the client's own diff and is not a field of the resource, leaving the object byte-for-byte what a non-watch read returns. Watch is refused outright on operator-authored declarative state, which changes only when somebody applies a change, rather than accepted as a poll that never prints a second line.
requirements.otherTestCoverage: ResourceWatchTest (14) against a real in-process cluster: a deployment applied, changed and deleted between ticks; a cordon landing mid-watch; NDJSON envelope shape; a server closed mid-watch giving up with the unreachable exit code; an unreachable first poll failing immediately; a non-watchable noun; a non-positive interval. Mid-watch mutations go over raw HTTP so they cannot pollute the asserted stdout buffer.

requirements.feature: Dry-run preview for a workload submission
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Fixed: closes FUNC-68. No mutating command had a preview path -- every one committed immediately -- and the only adjacent capability, gimle can-i, is explicitly RBAC-only and never checks quota, LimitRange or placement feasibility. A dry-run parameter on the workload PUT routes now runs RBAC, manifest parsing, artifact resolution, the admission chain and placement feasibility, returns a structured verdict naming each stage's outcome and the status the real request would have answered with, and proposes nothing to the store. The preview shares the real path rather than duplicating it, which is what makes it trustworthy: it calls the very same admission chain instances with the same arguments, and its failure detail is asserted to equal the real rejection response body byte for byte. Placement previously had four copies of candidate construction across the reconcilers; those were unified into one source that the reconcilers and the preview both use, so the preview cannot drift from what the reconciler will actually do. The scheduler's own placement function was verified to hold no store reference and mutate nothing, so it is safe to call from a preview directly. A rejected preview exits with the code the real submission would have used, because a pipeline gate whose exit status differs from the command it guards is useless; an unplaceable replica is the deliberate exception, warning on stderr at a zero exit, since no admission stage refuses a workload for being unschedulable -- the replica waits for room. Preview is refused with a clear message for kinds that have no admission chain or placement, rather than silently accepted.

requirements.feature: An instance observation carries the declared isolation tier and resource limit, so every read surface can show a usage figure against the ceiling it runs under
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Implemented. `ModuleDescriptor` declares `isolationTier` and `resourceLimit` and both are load-bearing at runtime (`AgentMain.prepareResourceLimit` turns the limit into the worker JVM's own `-Xmx`/`-XX:ActiveProcessorCount`), but neither was ever persisted or served: `InstanceObservation` carried `cpuMillicoresUsed`/`memoryBytesUsed` with no ceiling to read them against and no tier, so `GET /deployments`, `/daemonsets`, `/statefulsets` and `/jobs` -- all four sharing the single `ApiServer.observationToJson` -- could report a usage number but never a judgement. Both are now relayed as `Optional` fields along the pipe that already runs agent -> control plane -> store: `AgentMain.observationJson` reads them off the `ModuleDescriptor` the agent already retains on `SupervisedInstance`, `ApiServer` reads/writes them in its one shared observation codec, and `DomainCodec` encodes them onto the Raft-replicated heartbeat. Empty for a vessel instance, which is an OS process with no module descriptor behind it. A consumer must render the limit per tier or it misleads: at TIER_2 one instance owns its worker JVM so a used/limit ratio is correct, while at TIER_1 several instances share a JVM whose heap was sized for whichever instance spawned it, so the declared limit is what the manifest asked for rather than a bound applied to that instance. The record's seven telescoping constructors (arities 6 through 17, the shape that let a new field be silently defaulted at a call site) were replaced by a single canonical constructor plus an `InstanceObservation.builder(...)` taking the six facts a node can always report, with every measurable or declarable field defaulting to zero/empty until set; all 45 construction sites now build through it. M17 fix: none of this ever reached the console -- the deployment Instances table and instance detail page showed CPU/memory used with no limit and no tier anywhere. InstanceObservation/ModuleInstance (gimle-console's own TypeScript types) gained optional isolationTier/resourceLimit fields threaded through every mapping that already carries cpuMillicoresUsed/memoryBytesUsed, a new TierBadge component, and both read surfaces now show "used / limit" alongside a tier badge instead of a bare usage number with no denominator.

requirements.feature: An instance's own service-fabric address is readable through the control plane, so the fabric's listener-side defences can be exercised against a real cluster
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Implemented. A worker JVM's fabric TCP address (and its Unix-domain-socket path) arrives on the worker's own `Hello` handshake and lived only in the supervising agent's memory, reachable nowhere but SWIM gossip between agents -- not through any control-plane API, log, or CLI. That made the address undiscoverable from outside the node, which in turn made two shipped security behaviours impossible to prove end to end: exercising `FabricServer`'s listener-side tenant re-check, and deployment-scoped `NetworkPolicySpec` enforcement, both of which require dialing an instance directly to bypass the caller-side filter. `AgentLogServer` gained `GET /fabric-endpoints/{deploymentName}/{instanceIndex}`, reading the live `SupervisedInstance` state per request, and `ApiServer` gained `GET /instances/{name}/{index}/fabric-endpoint`, which resolves the hosting node across all four placement kinds and proxies there -- the same API-server-to-kubelet shape `/logs/instances/...` already uses. The agent distinguishes three outcomes rather than one 404: not supervised here (404), supervised but pre-handshake (409, so a caller retries rather than re-resolving), or the address (200). Read authorization is checked against the grant the instance's own owning workload kind falls under (`resolveInstanceNodeId` was widened to `resolveInstancePlacement`, reporting the kind alongside the node), so a DaemonSet or StatefulSet instance needs that kind's independently withholdable grant; an unresolvable instance is authorized before being answered, so 404-vs-403 cannot be used to probe which instances exist. Grants no new capability -- a fabric listener authenticates and authorizes every inbound call itself.

requirements.feature: Every control-plane API route is rate limited per source address, not only the unauthenticated CSR submission
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Implemented. `RequestRateLimiter` existed and was wired to exactly two things: the CSR submission route's per-address and cluster buckets, plus `LoginThrottle` on failed logins. Every other route -- including every write that proposes into Raft -- was unbounded, authenticated or not. The limiter is now charged inside `ApiServer#instrument`, the single wrapper every registered context already passes through, so no route can forget to opt in and a new one is covered by construction. A refused caller gets 429 with `Retry-After`, the same response shape the CSR and login paths already return. Keyed by remote address with deliberately no cluster-wide companion bucket, unlike the CSR pair: a shared bucket would let one flooding source spend the budget node agents' heartbeats draw from, and the control plane reads starved heartbeats as nodes going dark and answers with mass rescheduling -- turning a single-source flood into a cluster-wide outage, worse than the unbounded surface it set out to fix. Sized as a flood backstop rather than a quota (600-token burst, 5ms refill, ~200/s sustained per address), far above an agent's polling, an operator's bulk apply, or a console page load; tunable via `gimle.controlplane.rateLimit.burstPerAddress`/`.refillMillisPerAddress` and disableable via `.enabled=false`, which is the right setting when pointing `ragnarok stress` at a cluster. Console static assets are served outside `instrument` and are not charged.

requirements.feature: A Service may declare `protocol: UDP`, and gimle-bifrost relays it with per-client session tracking rather than only TCP streams
requirements.statusNote: New requirement: Implemented. `ServiceListener` relayed TCP only (`ServerSocket`/`Socket`), so no Service could front a DNS-shaped or any other datagram workload. `ServiceSpec` gained a `protocol` field (`ServiceProtocol.TCP|UDP`, the `Service.spec.ports[].protocol` analogue, TCP being what declaring none means), carried through `DomainCodec`, the `/services` API, the `/services/{name}/endpoints` payload Bifrost reads, and `gimle set service --protocol`. A UDP Service now binds `UdpServiceListener` instead. The hard part is reply routing: UDP has no connection, so every datagram arrives on one bound socket and the listener keeps a session per client address -- a dedicated upstream `DatagramSocket` connected to the selected backend plus a reader returning replies to that client -- reaped once idle past 60s, swept on the receive path rather than by a timer. Same shape kube-proxy's userspace UDP mode used. Two consequences documented rather than papered over: a session pins its backend for its lifetime whether or not `sessionAffinity` is declared (one upstream socket per client is what makes reply routing work; `sessionAffinity` instead decides how a *new* session picks its backend), and a UDP Service under a NetworkPolicy always fails closed, since a datagram relay has no handshake and no peer certificate from which to learn a caller's tenant -- the same permanent limit a plaintext TCP listener has, reached sooner because UDP has no TLS to opt into. Both listeners now sit behind a `ServiceRelay` interface so `BifrostProxy`'s poll loop drives either. Fixed alongside (M63): UdpServiceListener now binds unbound-then-explicit with SO_REUSEADDR (and best-effort SO_REUSEPORT) set before bind, so a Service at port==targetPort sharing its numeric port with a co-located wildcard-bound workload binds successfully instead of failing "Address already in use" on every poll tick.
